comment: The twelve of v2 (WISHLIST.md, The cast): id, name, role, ward, one of the three bodies on disk, and a `tint` hex every cloth material on that body is multiplied by (#419). Phase 6 is where they reach the screen, and it is where the Guard, the Scholar and the Wizard of v1 left it: `npcs`, the three the page used to spawn, is gone, and the riddle quest it played runs on the Constable until Phase 7 retires it. Dialogue is keyed by state: `default` is what everyone says, and the other states are the ones data/mystery.json's presses move an NPC to. src/mystery.js validates every press target and every statement source against these keys, and holds each `tint` to a #rrggbb.

cast.name: Sir Roger Lestrange

default: A clerk. A day early. Well, you have seen him, so you know what there is to know: the mason was drunk, the stair is steep, and he fell.
The King's inspector rides in tomorrow. I want a clean sheet by Vespers, and I want the mason buried before the inspector's horse is watered.
Ask what you must. Then come and tell me it was a fall.
{ACCUSE}

cast.dialogueComment: The last line is a token, the way the Scholar's used to end in {RIDDLE} (Phase 7). quest.json substitutes it, and `talked:constable` in `investigate` and `accusing` opens the accusation overlay after the conversation. validateAgainstNpcs holds the token and the action to each other in both directions.

default: The mason? A sad business. He drank, you know. They all do.
I sent no summons. Why would I? The chapel roof is sound, I have the ledger to say so.
If you want the works, the Clerk keeps the works. I keep the household.
admits: Where did you get that? No. Do not tell me.
I sent him to be talked to. By Robert. There was a matter of figures, and Robert wished to settle it like gentlemen.
To be talked to. Not to the stair. I never meant the stair.

default: Hywel. Yes. The best setter of stone in the March, and he could not set his own feet on a stair. A great loss to the works.
I was abed in my lodging from Compline. My boy will tell you. I heard of it at first light with everyone else.
The works are in order, if that is your errand. The lead is sheet-perfect. Count it yourself.
cloak: My cloak? That cloak has been in the laundry since Sunday. Ask the girl.
Tallow is tallow. There are a hundred candles in this castle and I have brushed past most of them.
cornered: Wastage. Yes. Wastage is a mason's word, clerk, not a thief's. Sheets crack. Sheets are cut short. Sheets are lost off a roof in a wind.
You have a ledger and an apprentice's memory. The Constable has a stair and a drunk. Ask yourself which he will write down.

default: Every soul through this gate goes in the book, clerk. Compline: the mason, on the Steward's word, about the chapel roof. Nobody else, in or out.
Gate barred behind him. And the walk door at my tower, barred as always.
You want to know how a man in the outer ward got to a stair in the inner? He did not. That is what the book is for.
admits: That door. God help me. I was in my cups, clerk, and it has not been barred this month, nor last.
You know what that is? A hanging matter, to say so. So I say it is barred, and I have said it so long I half believe it.

cast.name: Marged

default: Hywel took my lantern. The good one, off the kitchen hook, at Compline, and I told him bring it back and he said in the morning.
Called to the inner ward, he said. The chapel roof. At that hour. I said the roof will keep and he said the Steward would not.
And now I am short a lantern and a knife both. A knife gone since yesterday, off this table, and nobody knows a thing.
knife-hunting: A boning knife, a hand long, the haft bound with cord where it split. I would know it off any table in this castle.
Look in the bakehouse before you look at me. Everything that walks out of this kitchen walks that way first.
And the lantern. I have not forgotten the lantern, clerk, whatever else you find.
knife-found: The bakehouse. Of course the bakehouse. Flour on it, was there?
That is the boy. He takes it for the dough and leaves it in the trough and swears on his mother he never touched it.
So I am short a lantern and not a knife. And the lantern is the one that went up the Chapel Tower stair. Ask me about the lantern.
knife-settled: The knife is on its hook and the boy has had what I had for him.
My lantern is still out there, and the man who carried it off is laid out in the chapel.
Ask me about that one as often as you like.

cast.dialogueComment: The three knife states are the cook's-knife side quest's (data/quests/cooks-knife.json), not the mystery's. mystery.json grants `cook-lantern` and `knife-missing` off `default` and off nothing else, and the engine reads its own `st.pressed` rather than the line set on screen, so none of these three can grant a clue however the quest walks. test/quest.mjs holds every dialogue key on every npc to a stage or a press that can reach it, the side quests now included.
cast.dialogue2Comment: The knife thread is day one's. On the morning after `_dayLines` replaces every line set in this file, which is why there is no Lauds variant of any of the three.

default: I found him with the Constable at first light. I have said the office for him. There is nothing more I can do for him now.
My chamber is above the stair. I sleep sound, clerk. I heard nothing.
Sir Roger says a fall. Sir Roger is the King's Constable.
And since you are the King's clerk and count things for a living: I am a candle short. Four tallow in the aumbry at Compline, three at Lauds. It is not a matter. I mention it.
candle-short: Four tallow, of the kitchen's making, in the aumbry by the vestry door, and the aumbry has no lock because who would rob a chapel of tallow. Three this morning.
I keep the account for the exchequer's man. A candle a week for the office and one over for a burial. He will not care for one candle. I care for a column that does not add.
I did not take it up to my chamber; I have said I sleep sound. Look on the stair if you like. I do not use the stair after Compline, and I have not looked.
candle-found: In the pricket at the first turn. That pricket has stood empty since Sir Walter's day. The office is said below, and nobody carries a light past the turn but me.
Then my four is four, and somebody stood at the turn of my stair long enough to pool a candle's worth of tallow on the step. That is not a moment. That is a man waiting.
Enter it in your column, clerk. I have my own to keep, and it adds now, which I find is not what I wanted.
candle-entered: The column adds. One tallow, taken up the stair by a hand not mine, burnt to the socket. I have written it so.
I have said the office for him twice now. I find I have not finished saying it.
If you have anything the Steward has said that you would put to me, put it. I have been a coward once this week and I would rather not be asked to be one twice.
heard: The Steward said that? Then God forgive me, I will say what I heard.
Two men on the stair at the second bell. Voices, low, then not low. Then one man, going up. Only one.
I lay and listened to one man go up my stair and I did not get out of my bed. That is what I heard nothing means.

cast.name: Dafydd ap Rhys
cast.role: Garrison, night watch on the north walk

default: North walk, Compline to Lauds, every night this month. You see the whole north side from the Kitchen Tower door.
Second bell, a man went east along the walk past my post. Fur-trimmed cloak. I know fur when the moon is on it.
The Clerk's the only man in the works with fur on him. I thought he was walking off a supper. I wish I had stopped him.
And since you go through the gate and I do not: Gwilym has four pence of mine at dice, and he has stopped playing and started asking. Tell him Saturday. Tell him I said it civil.
dice-owed: Four pence. It was two, then a throw for the two, and it was four. His dice, his lodge, his ale, at Lauds when the watch is done and the gate opens. I have not been through that lodge door since, nor will I till I have the four.
He sits in there all day and all night with the book and the bar and the jug, and he does not forget a penny, that man, whatever else he forgets.
Saturday. Say it so he hears it, clerk. He is a hard man to make hear a thing he does not want to.
dice-told: You told him. And he said nothing, I would wager. That is Gwilym. He writes a thing down and says nothing.
I will pay him Saturday and I will not sit at his table again, not at Lauds nor any other hour. That is my word and you may write it in your book.
You have been in his lodge, then, and seen him with the jug. Then you know what a bar looks like to a man who has been at the jug since Compline. I say no more than that.
dice-bar: He has said it, then. About the bar. God help him, and I say that meaning it.
It has leaned on that wall since Lammas. Every man who walks the north walk has seen it lean there and every man of us has said the door is Gwilym's and not ours.
And I owed him four pence and held my tongue about it, and you may write that against me too. A man went east past my post at the second bell and that door was open at the far end of his walk.
dice-paid: Saturday, and civil, and four pence he will have, and then I keep to my own walk and he keeps to his lodge.
North walk, Compline to Lauds, from the Kitchen Tower door. That is my post and I was at it.
Second bell, a man in a fur-trimmed cloak went east along it past me. I have said that to you already and I will say it to whoever asks.

cast.heldPropComment: Dafydd is the only one of the twelve carrying anything. The mace came into the project on the Guard of v1 and stays referenced through him; it is also what reads as a soldier from across the ward, where a tint alone does not.

default: Drunk? Hywel? Not on a working day, clerk, and yesterday was one. Not a drop after the Sunday bell and not a drop till Saturday.
He kept his own count of the lead. Eleven tally sticks on his belt, a notch a sheet. Two hundred and twelve laid, by his count, and he was going to show somebody.
He went out of the lodge at Compline with the sticks on him. I know because he told me mind the fire.

His tools lie where he left them, that is the custom, and I am the one that takes them up. Only the good chisel is not among them. Madoc had it for a new edge, and Madoc is in the tower, and nobody will let a lodge boy by the bars to ask him.
chisel-asking: Ash haft, a hand and a half long, his mark on the tang. He cut every head in the chapel with it. Nobody has had it in hand in four years but him and me, and me only to carry it.

Madoc draws the lodge's chisels twice a year for ale, that is the custom, and that one went to him a week since with an edge on it like a spoon. Then they took him up the tower and the forge went cold.
You are the King's man. They will let you by the bars. Ask him where he left it. That is all I want. I will finish the head he was on, and then I will lay my course at Michaelmas as he said I would.
chisel-heard: You went in to him. And he gave you the lead and the cart and the Clerk's seal, and not one word about a chisel. That is Madoc. He has said the same three things to every man who has stood at those bars for eleven days.
Then it is in the tower with him or wherever he put it, and I will not wait on it.
There is a stone in the lodge and I have watched him draw an edge two years running. Mine will not be his. It will cut.
chisel-forge: Out to the forge at Prime and in at Vespers, eight days of the eleven, and the roll says so? Then it never went up the tower at all. It is at the forge, on the bench or in the trough, where he works and not where he sleeps.
Nobody stops a lodge boy at a forge. I will be there at Prime tomorrow when they walk him down, and he will hand it me over the wall as he has a hundred times.
You had that off a barrel-head in the guardroom, and not one man of the garrison thought to read it in eleven days. The lodge can count. It seems the lodge can read as well.
chisel-own-edge: I put an edge on the second chisel myself, on the lodge stone, and it took me till the bell. It is not Madoc's edge. It cuts.
The head he was on is a king's, for the springing of the chapel arch. I will finish it as he began it and set the small cross under it as he did, and the chaplain need not know.
He told me mind the fire. I have minded it. The rest I am learning.
chisel-fetched: Prime tomorrow, at the forge, and I will have it off him. I have his mark on the tang and the custom on my side, and now the roll, which is the King's.
I will finish the head he was on with his own iron. That is how it should be done, and I had given it up.
He told me mind the fire. I have minded it.

default: That cloak? The Clerk's. His boy brought it down at first light and said wash it and say nothing.
It goes in the copper at Sext with the rest. If you want to look at it, look now.
wife: Madoc is my husband. Yes. Since you ask what nobody else has.
They put him in the tower for the lead because somebody had to go in the tower. I have no reason on this earth to lie for the Clerk of Works, and one very good one to lie against him.
So weigh what I say however you like. The cloak is still the Clerk's.

default: Another one come to look at the thief. Look, then.
The lead went out the gate on a cart, by daylight, with the Clerk's seal on the pass. I saw it go. I said so. That is why I am here.
Nobody believes a smith in a tower. You will not either. Go on.
forge: You have had the roll off the barrel-head. Somebody in this castle can read, then.
Eight days at the forge and I watched that cart both ways. It came in empty and it went out with the axle riding low, and I have shod that horse eleven years. It was not stone.
And the dates are in that roll and they have been in it for eleven days. Show it to the Constable. He will tell you a smith is a smith and a roll is a roll.

default: Wykes, of the town. I have the cart contract for the works.
Dressed stone. I buy stone off the works and sell it on. That is the whole of my trade, clerk.
The cart? Sacking and stone. Mind your boots.
admits: You have been under the sacking. Well.
The Clerk sells. The Steward signs the pass. I only buy, clerk, and a man who only buys has hanged for less, so I will be in the town by Sext and you may tell them I said so.

default: The King's clerk, in my chamber, about a mason. My husband will be so pleased.
Piers Marrable? He writes his sevens like gallows. Everyone in this ward knows his hand; he signs everything, and he signs it large.
My window looks over the inner ward. I see a great deal from it and I am asked about none of it.

And if you are going up on the walk, which everybody seems to be today: my merlin slipped her jesses at Prime and sits on the south walk as if she had bought it. The sentry will not fetch her. A post is a post, he says.
hawk-loose: Ffion. A merlin, a year to my hand, and she went off the sill at Prime with her jesses trailing and sat down on the south walk by the Bakehouse Tower as if she had bought it.
I sent to the sentry. A post is a post, he says, and the King did not put him on the north walk to chase a lady's bird along the south one. He is right. I find I mind that he is right.
Go up by the Bakehouse Tower door. If she is on the parapet do not reach for her; tell me where she sits and I will send the boy with the lure.
hawk-seen: You went up. No, do not tell me: the parapet over the Bakehouse Tower door, which is the one place the boy cannot get a ladder to.
She came back to the sill an hour after you went, on her own, as they do when the ward is quiet and nobody is looking at them. So you climbed for nothing, and I am obliged to you for it.
You have seen the south walk by daylight, then, which most of this castle never has. It is a long way from the Bakehouse Tower door to anywhere, and nobody up there is written in any book.
hawk-home: She is on her block and sulking, and you went where the sentry would not. I do not forget that kind of thing.
The wards are one ward up on that walk, clerk. I have said so before and nobody has asked me what I meant by it.
My window looks over the inner ward. I see a great deal from it. Ask.
window: You have been up on the walk. Then you know what I know, that the wards are one ward up there.
Last night: one lantern going up the Chapel Tower stair, late. And after, a shadow along the south walk, going westward, with no lantern at all.
I did not think it my business. I have been married to a Constable eleven years.

cast.name: Master Adam Fraunceys
cast.arrivesComment: THE THIRTEENTH, AND HE IS NOT IN THE CASTLE ON DAY ONE (#534). `arrives: 2` is what tells src/mystery.js not to ask him for a day-one schedule and src/quest-manager.js to keep him out of the accusation panel: twelve names and a fall is the choice the Constable offers, and a man who has not dismounted yet is not one of them. His lines for the morning after are in mystery.json's `day2.lines`, keyed by what the player said, and not here, because there are seven of them and which one he speaks is a fact about the mystery rather than about the body. The one `default` line below is the fallback and is only reachable if `applyDay` never ran.

default: The King's inspector has not dismounted yet.

chatterComment: WISHLIST.md theme 3 (#554, expanded #558): ambient talk, for the existing twelve only, no new bodies. Twenty-seven pairs. Two populace members within earshot at one bell get a line pair from the pool for their ward and that watch, played as a floating caption; this repo has no populace yet, so today the pool is unused by the game and exists for src/lore.js to validate and for a later populace row to spend. Keyed by ward (both npcs' own `ward` field, above) then watch. Each pair carries the two speakers by id (order is speaking order), the two lines, and an optional `cites`: the lore ids the exchange tells, which data/lore.json's `sources` point back at by this pair's own id.

lines: Marged: That cousin of yours reads a frost off a cat's back better than any almanac I ever paid for.
Nest: She is no cousin of mine past what the roll says, and I never said the charm was worth the penny. I never said it wasn't, either.
Ieuan: Hywel cuts a little cross at the springing of every arch. Cadeyrn's mark, he calls it, same as his father did.
Master Robert: Saint Osyth keeps this chapel, Ieuan. Saint Cadeyrn keeps nothing but a mason's conscience, and a light one at that.
Dafydd: There is a cross cut in the stone for every man who died building this place. Count them and you have the priest's roll without the Latin.
Ieuan: A cross goes at the springing of an arch, Dafydd, and it means the arch. The watch has counted them twice and got two numbers, and neither of them was the roll.
Master Robert: Eleven miles is a long way to haul stone for a market day, Wykes.
Thomas Wykes: Eleven miles is nothing beside the quay toll Mereford pays to send it back out again.
Ieuan: A hod-carrier went off the Bakehouse Tower's scaffold in the ninth year and stood up laughing, they say, for calling on Cadeyrn on the way down.
Thomas Wykes: They also say it was a load of straw broke his fall and not the saint. I have hauled that straw. It was a great deal of straw.
Nest: Madoc drew out every chisel in that lodge at Lady Day and took a jug of ale for it, and the Steward wrote the jug down as a loss.
Ieuan: Twice a year, Lady Day and Michaelmas, his father before him at the same forge under the Prison Tower wall. Hywel called it the one custom in this castle the King had not paid for.
Marged: Nest says the well tastes of rock and she draws from it every day of her life. That is the whole of what I know about the well.
Dafydd: They say it goes down to the river and the tide comes up in it, and a man with a boat and a sack could poison the castle from the quay. Nobody who says it has lowered a light.
Ieuan: Hywel was carrying stone up this castle at nine years old. Nine, Nest, the year his own father died on the scaffold.
Nest: And keeps a tally stick at his belt to this day for it, so nobody ever tells him at the week's end that he wasn't paid for what he carried.
Dafydd: My grandfather swore the chapel bell was a shrine bell off the March once, melted down so no native hand would ring it.
Marged: Your grandfather swore a great many things, Dafydd ap Rhys, and I never saw him show me the shrine.
Madoc: Something moves under this floor at night. Slow. A drag, then a stop, same as it has since before they put me in to hear it.
Nest: You have said that every day this week, Madoc, and I have believed you every day this week, and neither of those has got you out.

Dafydd: My grandfather stood on the other bank of this river against the old King for nine years, Wykes, and was sworn at the end of it, and kept his word and his opinions both. I stand the King's watch and I have the opinions.
Thomas Wykes: And the song, I suppose. I have heard the garrison sing it over the wall at Michaelmas for twenty years and never been told a word of what it says.
Dafydd: Not one man of the watch will draw from the south-west well after dark. Not one, and every one of them a different reason why.
Marged: The water tastes the same to me at any hour, and I am the one who has actually tried it after dark.
Nest: The inner ward eats first, warms first and is paid first, Master Robert, whatever the works go without.
Master Robert: The inner ward would say the same of you and mean the opposite. That is the whole of what a wall is for.

Marged: Michaelmas day the town has this whole ward by charter, Prime to Vespers, stalls from the lodge to the hall, and the garrison stands on the walk and watches its own yard fill up with the people it keeps out the rest of the year.
Nest: And for one day the only tongue in the outer ward is our own, and the inner ward stands at its gate and does not understand a word, and that is the best of it.
Gwilym: Three months owed again, Master Piers, same as the last time and the time before that.
Piers Marrable: The King's coin goes where the King is fighting, Gwilym. It is paid in the end. It is always paid in the end.
Father Anselm: A cold night for the walk, my lady.
Lady Alys: Every night is a cold night on that walk, Father. I have stopped remarking on it.
Gwilym: They say the old King's heart is under your altar stone, Father, in a lead box sent up from Vantry the year he died, so that some part of him should see the place finished.
Father Anselm: I have had a bar under that stone once, Gwilym, and I will not tell you what I found, because whichever way it went it is a scandal, and I have enough of those.
Piers Marrable: The Sunder War is two years settled, Sir Roger. When does the coin catch up with the peace?
Sir Roger: When Caernarfon says it does. I have stopped asking twice a year and started asking once.
Gwilym: They say Sir Walter's own coffer covered what the works had lost, before he died, and that's the whole reason his books balanced.
Father Anselm: I have read his accounts, Gwilym. I have also heard what you just said from three other mouths, each swearing he had it from a fourth.
Piers Marrable: There is an alderman's family in Mereford that has not paid its wall-tax in a decade, if the roll were ever made to say so.
Gwilym: And whose hand keeps the roll from saying so, Master Piers? I only ask because I keep a roll myself.
Sir Roger: You came up from Caernarfon, Father. Twelve years, is it. You could go back.
Father Anselm: A younger son with good Latin and no living, Sir Roger. The justiciar's chapel has a dozen of those. This one has a roll nobody else can read and a stair nobody else sleeps over.
Sir Roger: Give the outer ward its head and it would drink the cellar dry and leave the walk door standing open besides.
Piers Marrable: A firm hand is the whole of what keeps this castle a castle and not a March village with better stone around it, Sir Roger. I have always said so.
Lady Alys: You look tired, Father.
Father Anselm: I have a deal of praying still to do today, my lady, and the day is not half over.
Lady Alys: Eleven years married, Father, and eight of them here. Sir Roger had twelve men at Bryn Adda and thought himself a Constable. He has eight now and a wall, and thinks himself less of one.
Father Anselm: And a wife whose brother sits among the justiciar's clerks, my lady, which he has never once mentioned and never once forgotten.
Sir Roger: That wall of yours was not in the engineer's drawing, Gwilym. He put it in the fourth year, after a muster showed him five March men in the yard to every one of the King's.
Gwilym: And my father kept the gate in it from the day it stood, Sir Roger, and I have kept it since. A castle inside a castle, the engineer called it. A wall with a door in it, my father called it.
Father Anselm: I keep a knuckle of bone under glass on the north sill, my lady, and call it Saint Osyth's own.
Lady Alys: And do you believe that, Father, or only say it?
Father Anselm: On my better days, both.

Piers Marrable: Two offices, two men, two rings of keys, since the day they opened Sir Walter's books. The exchequer's man ordered it standing in that chamber and Sir Roger has kept to it as if he thought of it.

Gwilym: One man held both for two and thirty years and nobody could check him. My father said Sir Walter never once locked the household's door, because there was no one to lock it against but himself.

performancesComment: WISHLIST.md theme 3's two set pieces, BACKLOG.md rank 8 (#592): lore performed rather than read. Two pools, `sermons` and `songs`. Each entry is one person speaking or singing alone in one room at one bell, played as the caption band src/ui.js draws (the same band the `chatter` pool above is waiting for), once, to whoever is standing in the room to hear it. A pool is flat rather than nested the way `chatter` is, because a performance names its own `room` and `watch` and a chatter pair names neither. `npc` is who performs it and has to be somebody data/mystery.json's own schedule puts in that room at that watch: the sermon is said where the chaplain is, not where a data file wishes he were. `watch` is one of the four bells, or `lauds`, the morning after (data/mystery.json's `day2.watch`), which is how a pool tells a second day something the first day did not hear. `lines` are said in order, one caption at a time; a line in brackets is what the room does rather than what the speaker says. `cites` are the lore ids the piece tells, and data/lore.json's own `sources` name the piece back by id, the way they do for a document or a chatter pair. THE THIRD POOL (#648): `rumours`, what the castle is saying about the player on the morning after. A rumour piece may carry `when`, `unless` and `knew` on the same grammar data/mystery.json's `day2.castle` and `day2.knew` use (src/mystery.js's `dayTwoApplies`), so which one is said is the verdict the player reached and the journal he carried into it; `knew` names clues he has to be holding, all of them. Only a `lauds` piece may carry them, because a verdict is a thing only the morning after has, and src/lore.js refuses one at any of the four bells. That turns the old rule here into an order: a room at a bell holds a LIST, in file order, and the first piece whose conditions the play answers is the one said. Narrowest first, always, because src/lore.js refuses any piece the ones above it answer for in every ending and journal, which is the same rail as before with seven mornings in it instead of one. The three below are the guardroom at Lauds, Dafydd off watch and awake, and the narrow one is keyed on the gaol roll being in the journal: it is the one thing the castle can only say to a player who did the work. WHERE THE SONG GOES (#593): WISHLIST.md asked for a song in the hall at Sext and the schedule puts nobody in the Great Hall at Sext, so the hall's song is sung at Vespers, which is the one bell both wards eat there (`hall-high-table`), and a second song went into the kitchen at Sext so that day one has a piece to find before its last bell.

lines: The office of Vespers, said to whoever came, and the whole of the rest of this castle at its supper in the hall.
Sit, Ieuan. Saint Osyth heard smaller congregations than this one in her own lifetime, and hers were out of doors.
She is the King's own house's saint, and so she is this chapel's, as she is every chapel the crown has raised in the March these forty years.
Every soul under this floor is commended to her in my Latin, whatever was said over them first, and in whatever tongue it was said.
Sir Walter Esturmy lies under this floor, where he asked to be. Two and thirty years Constable, and he paid the last of the works' stone to lay the flags he is under.
His accounts balanced to the penny when the exchequer opened them after him. I have said that from this step before now and I will go on saying it.
[a pause, and the candle on the north sill gutters and holds]
Now the Magnificat, and then go and eat, boy. Your master would not thank me for keeping you off your supper.
They keep my place below the salt until I come down to it. They have kept it for one chaplain or another these forty years and they will not be giving it away tonight.
The grave is filled, and the office is said, and I have yet to find that either of those is the same thing as finished.
The works were here at first light, before I was down my own stair. They said their own words over him and I let them say them.
They keep Cadeyrn, who was known on this ground before the King's masons ever were: patron of builders, and of men who work in high places.
So I say Osyth's Latin over the top of theirs, the way the walk goes over the cross-wall, and in twelve years I have not once seen the two get in each other's way.
He was a boy of nine on these scaffolds the year his father came off them. Forty years of this castle has had that one family's hands somewhere on it.
[the bell is not rung; it is too early in the day for it]
Requiem aeternam dona ei, Domine. What the sheet says of him is the sheet's business. This is mine.
[Marged keeps the time on the board with the heel of her hand]
Forty to feed and the one oven lit, and eight of them sworn and no use of it;
a dozen to the works and the town at noon, and the inner ward calling for theirs too soon.
The second oven is a store, and has been a store since the building years, and I have not got the men to fire it if it were not.
Eleven years I have stood at this board. In eleven years that fire has not once gone out on me, whatever else in this castle has.
[the pot goes on, and the tune goes on under it, with no more words to it]
[Dafydd is got up onto the bench end, and the benches take up the time with their cups]
Forty Michaelmas, and the roof not on, and the King that began it dead and gone;
six for the curtain and ten for the towers, and the rest of it built in the King's spare hours!
Eight men watching where eighty stood, and three months' wages made good in wood!
[the high table laughs half a beat late; the Constable's cup goes down an inch and comes back up]
There is a verse about a writ, and a verse about a river. Those two I do not sing in the King's tongue.
[he sings them anyway, and the benches have every word of them, and the high table has none]

rumours.why: The sharpest thing the castle can say about the player, and the only one it cannot say unless the player did the work: the roll was read, off the barrel-head in this room, and the smith was named anyway.
lines: [Dafydd has the barrel-head to himself and is not cleaning anything on it]
You will want the roll. It is not here. The King's man had it up at first light and he has not sent it back down.
I told him where it had been lying. I told him who had had it off the barrel-head yesterday, because he asked me and I will not lie to a man with a sheet in front of him.
You read those dates. I watched you read them. Eleven days, out at Prime and in at Vespers and shut at Compline, in my own hand and my own hours.
And then you went up to the Constable and you said the smith.
They have it in the outer ward that you came up from Caernarfon to find a man to hang and found one. I am not saying it. I am telling you it is being said.
[he puts his hand flat on the barrel-head where the roll was lying, and leaves it there]

rumours.why: Nobody hanged, so the castle has nothing to hang the clerk's day on either. A day of questions with no name at the end of it is the one shape this castle finds hardest to make a story out of, and it makes two.
lines: [Dafydd is at the barrel-head with the roll open and nothing written in it since the night before]
Nothing this morning. No rope, no hole in the ground, no name read out. I have stood a first light like it twice in twenty years and neither of them sat right either.
The works have it that you asked every soul in this castle a question and took none of the answers. The inner ward has it that you were told what to find and had the sense not to find it.
I have my own. You asked me the same thing three times and the third time you asked it differently, which is not a man who has been told anything.
Master Fraunceys signs at noon that Hywel ap Gruffudd was a drunk who came off his own scaffold. Father Anselm will go on saying he heard two men on that stair.
Come Michaelmas there will be nobody left who stands still for the chaplain, and there will still be nobody in the ground for it.
[he shuts the roll]

rumours.why: The general case: somebody hanged this morning on what the clerk carried up the stair, and the castle has settled on two versions of the clerk that will both outlast him. It is written last because the two above it are the plays it must not answer for.
lines: [Dafydd is at the barrel-head, and the guardroom is a room short of one man this morning]
It was done before the bell. They do it before the bell so the works are not on the wall for it, and the works were on the wall for it anyway.
You will hear what is being said about you. You may as well hear it from somebody who will say it to your face.
The outer ward has you for the King's own hand: came up from Caernarfon, walked about for a day asking after a dead mason, and a man hanged for it at first light.
The inner ward has you for a clerk who did what a clerk is sent to do and will be gone by noon. That is the kinder of the two and I would not take much comfort in it.
Gwilym wrote you in at the gate on a pass like anybody else. That is the whole of what this castle actually knows about you, and it has not stopped one of them.
[he goes back to the roll, and does not look up again]

reputationComment: REPUTATION BY WARD (BACKLOG.md rank 8, #599 named the wards and this block is what reads them). The save carries two counters, `outer` and `inner`, one moved per side quest finished in that ward, and this is one of the two things in the game that can tell they moved; the other is the closing pane, which is `closing` below. THIS IS A TINT AND NOT A SYSTEM (WISHLIST.md, theme 4): nothing here gates, grants, hides or unlocks anything, and a player who runs no errand at all sees none of it and loses nothing. `outer` and `inner` are each a list of `{at, line}` in ascending order of `at`. `at` is how many errands in that ward have to be finished for the line to be the one said; the highest threshold reached wins, and below the first one nobody says anything. The line goes on the END of whatever the person you are talking to says, the way each errand's opener went on the end of a `default` set (#598, and the same reason: the line is last, so a player re-reading what came before it is not made to). WHO SAYS IT IS THE WARD AND NOT THE PERSON. Any of the cast whose own `ward` matches, in whatever state they are standing in, which is why every line below has to be sayable by a cook, a sentry and a man in a cell, or by a Constable, a chaplain and a lady. That is what makes it the castle talking rather than one more person with an errand. Day one only, and never on a press: the morning after replaces every line set in this file (data/mystery.json's `day2.lines`) and a press is the mystery answering a clue the player pushed at somebody, which is no place for the castle's gossip. `closing` is keyed to the two counters added together and is the one line the epilogue pane carries under the verdict. `validateQuestSet` (src/quest-graph.js) holds every `at` to the number of quests data/quests/ actually has in that ward, so a threshold nobody could ever reach fails test/quest.mjs rather than sitting here silent; three outer and two inner today, so the ceilings are 3, 2 and 5.

outer.line: And there is talk of you in the yard between the kitchen and the lodge. A King's man who carries a thing for a man who asked him, and does not write it down after. We had not looked for that today of all days.
The outer ward knows your face now, clerk, and not for the sheet you are writing. Whatever name goes on it at Vespers, there will be somebody down here who says you were fair with us.

inner.line: And it is noticed, what you did this morning, small as it was. Little enough is noticed in this ward that was not asked for twice.

You have made yourself useful in this ward twice over and asked nothing back either time. That is remarked on above stairs. Whether it is remarked on kindly you will know at Vespers, with the rest of us.

closing.line: Between the bells you did something for somebody who could not do it themselves, and there is no line on the sheet for it.

The sheet carries the mason and nothing else. It does not carry the errands you ran between the bells, and the kitchen and the gate and the lodge will carry those longer than Caernarfon carries the sheet.

Every favour anybody in this castle thought to ask of a passing clerk, you did, and not one of them is on the sheet. Nobody who asked has forgotten. That is the other record, and it stays in the ward.
